[[File:Indian thorny bamboo (Bambusa bambos) in the Singapore Botanic Gardens.jpg|thumb|right|in the Singapore Botanic Gardens]]
'''''Bambusa bambos''''', (synonym '''Gigantichloa maxima''') the '''giant thorny bamboo''', '''Indian thorny bamboo''', '''spiny bamboo''', or '''thorny bamboo''' (but see ''[[Bambusa spinosa]]'')<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.feedipedia.org/node/496 | title=Giant thorny bamboo (Bambusa bambos) | Feedipedia}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | url=https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/8399 | title=Bambusa bambos (giant thorny bamboo)| date=2022| doi=10.1079/cabicompendium.8399| last1=Rojas-Sandoval| first1=J.| work=CABI Compendium| volume=CABI Compendium| page=8399| doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://eol.org/pages/1114097/details|title=Indian Thorny Bamboo - Encyclopedia of Life}}</ref> is a species of clumping [[bamboo]] native to southern [[Asia]] ([[India]], [[Pakistan]], [[Bangladesh]], [[Sri Lanka]] and [[Indochina]]). It is also naturalized in [[Seychelles]], [[Central America]], [[West Indies]], [[Java]], [[Malaysia]], [[Maluku (province)|Maluku]], and the [[Philippines]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/?name_id=398642 |access-date=2023-04-27 |website=Plants of the World Online |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Ohrnberger|first=Dieter|title=The bamboos of the world: annotated nomenclature and literature of the species and the higher and lower taxa|year=1999|publisher=Elsevier|isbn=978-0-444-50020-5|page=255}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Pakistan gears up for Green Growth: Finalising the National Bamboo Strategy - Story {{!}} IUCN |url=https://iucn.org/story/202410/pakistan-gears-green-growth-finalising-national-bamboo-strategy |access-date=2026-03-13 |website=iucn.org |language=en}}</ref>
<!-- Plant is known as "ක‍ටු උණ - katu una" in Sri Lanka, by Sinhalese people. -->

==Habit==
It is a tall, bright-green colored spiny bamboo species, which grows in thickets consisting of a large number of heavily branched, closely growing culms. It reaches a height of 10–35 m and grows naturally in the forests of the dry zones. It is very fast growing, lengthening up to 50 cm in the twelve night-time hours.<ref>{{cite book | last= De la Rue | first= E.Aubert | date= 1957 | title= The Tropics | location= New York | publisher= Alfred A. Knopf| page= 106}}</ref> Since most of the growth is at night, it probably practices [[Crassulacean Acid Metabolism]] or CAM. The record growth for this species is 90 cm in 24 hours at Kew Gardens near London in 1855.<ref>{{cite book | last= Arbor | first= Agnes B. |date= 1934 | title= The Graminae - A Study of Cerial, Bamboo and Grasses | location= Cambridge, England | publisher= Cambridge Univ. Press | page= 62}}</ref>

==Appearance==
[[File:18th century illustration flora of the coast of Coromandel Coast India Plants Fruits Flowers (10).jpg|thumb|Illustration of leaves, fruits and flowers.]]
The culms are not straight, and are armed with stout, curved spines. They are bright green, becoming brownish green when drying, and the young shoots are deep purple. Branches spread out from the base. Aerial roots reach up to few nodes above. The internode length is 15–46 cm, and diameter is 3.0–20 cm, and the culm walls are 2.5–5.0 cm thick. Nodes are prominent and [[rootstock]] is stout.

Culm sheaths are dark brown when mature, elongated, and cylindrical. Length of the sheath proper is 15–25 cm and 12–30 cm in width. Blade length is 4.0–12 cm. Auricles are not prominent. Upper surfaces of the sheath are covered with blackish-brown hairs. Lower surfaces of the sheath are not hairy. Sheaths fall early.

==Uses==
They are extensively used in many applications, mainly for making bridges and for ladders. Leaves are used for [[thatching]].
